7. The suit was contested by the defendant Nos.l-4 who filing written statement denying the materials allegation made in the plaint. The case of the defendants are, in short, is that the plaintiff is out of possession from the date of execution of Hebabil ewaz dated 23.10.1983 and from then the plaintiff is nobody for the suit land. Thus the plaintiff has filed the present suit after 19 years 2 months and 7 days. The defendants have acquired title by adverse possession from 23.10.1983. Since the plaintiff is out of possession from 1983 the suit is not maintainable at her instance. The plaintiff is a shrewd and cunning woman who at the instance of others have filed the suit for illegal gain. Abdus Samad Parai the predecessor of the defendant was a man of choice and solvate. He did not plough his own land and borga cultivate the land of others. He did not also borga cultivate the land of the plaintiff. The vexatious suit of the plaintiff is liable to be dismissed with costs. 

 17. He also submits that it is not comet to say that the identity of the survey related with the khatian and plot numbers of the suit land have not been given in the plaint. He referring the plaint submits that the khatian and plot numbers are related with the settlement khatian. In this connection he also submits that when the first record of right was started under the provision of Bengal Tenancy Act in some of the area of our country. The first record of right is known as C.S record of right, that is, Cadstale Survey and in some district the same survey is known as settlement khatian. In the area of Mymensingh the first survey is know as settlement khatian and the same has been given in the pleadings. He candidly admits that it is fact that in the schedule of the plaint there is no identity of the survey and the same should have been there and if it would have been their, their would have no scope to create any confusion and unwanted debit on this fact. 

 18. He also submits that in the record of right there appears no name of the concerned survey. After C.S. record of right in many area of our country revisional survey, that is, R.S. record of right and after coming operation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the S.A record of right has been prepared but in no record of right, the name of the survey has been articulated by the authority. So, it is not a ground for disbelieving the case of the plaintiff. 

 25. Now, let us have a look-what is adverse possession in the eye of law. In the case of Secretary of State for India vs Devendra Lal Khan reported in 61 I A.78=38 C W N.. 285, the Privy Council laid down what constitutes adverse possession and observed in the following ways: "As to what constitutes adverse possession, a subject which formed the topic of some discussion in the case, their Lordships adopt the language of Lord Robertson in delivering the judgment of the Board in Radhamoni Devi Vs Collector of Khulna" (27 I.A. 136), where his Lordship said that the possession required must be adequate in continuity, in publicity and in extent to show that it is possession adverse to the competitor . It is sufficient that the possession should be overt and without any attempt at concealment so that the person against whom time is running ought, if he exercises due vigilance, to be aware of what is happening." 

 26. The jest of the adverse possession as observed by the Privy Council is that the possession must be continuous having knowledge to others and it must have an expose against the real owner. In my consideration, the written statement of the defendants and their claim of possession in to the suit land from 1983 through the deed of Hebabil ewaz allegedly executed by the plaintiff is sufficient to hold that the possession of the defendants from 1983 is not any adverse possession at all rater the possession that have been claimed by the defendant themselves is based on the so-called deed of gift and this sort of possession can never be adverse possession against the real owner. 

 29. In the case of Abdus Samad and others Vs. Deputy Commissioner and Custodian of the Vested Property and Non Resident Property, Munshigong reported in 5 MLR (AD)73 it was held that permissive possession of a party is not a adverse possession against the real owner. In the reported case, I find that the suit land of that suit originally belonged to Gobinda Chandra Dutta and others who had left this country for India some timing 1920 making over its possession daily to one Lal Mia who possessed the some for over 65 years without any interruption from any quarter. After his death the plaintiffs having been possessing the suit land for over 12 years and thus they have acquired title thereto by way of adverse possession and the defendants have no right, title or possession therein but they had most illegally enlisted the suit property as vested property, hence that suit was filed for declaration that the enlistment of the property as vested property is illegal and that the plaintiffs have title thereto by way of adverse possession. The vested property authority appearing in the said suit stated that the suit property has been correctly enlisted as vested property as the owners thereof had left for India and the government is in possession thereof through its lessee. In the trial the suit was dismissed by the Senior Assistant Judge but in the appeal, the appellate Court reversed the decision of the trial Court and decreed the suit. Against the judgment of the appellate Court below a civil revision was preferred in the High Court Division and this Division setting aside the judgment of the appellate Court below restored the judgment of the trial Court. Thereafter, leave was sought for before the Appellate Division whether plaintiffs' possession in to the suit land can be considered as adverse possession. The Appellate Division ultimately found that Lal Mia was always permissive possessor and his such possession cannot be considered as adverse possession in order to create title. The observations of the Appellate Division runs as follows: 

 30. In the reported case Lal Mia and his heirs were in possession of the suit land more than 75 years but even then they did not acquire title in to the suit land by adverse possession as that was not adverse and hostile against the real owner and as against the government also. I find similarity between the fact of the reported case and the case in my hands. In the instant case, the defendants were allegedly inducted in to possession of the suit land as borgader of the plaintiff to borga cultivate her land. But, in the written statement it has been articulated that the father of the defendants  was a luxurious man and he did not plough his own land, rather he employing labors use to cultivate his land. So, he did not take any land from the plaintiff for borga cultivation. If the case of the defendants is taken as a fact that he was not engaged as borga cultivator in that event also since the defendants were allegedly possessing the suit land on the strength of an illegal Hebabil ewaz their such possession would not be adverse possession at any point of time against the real owner. But their possession had become adverse on 27.08.20(8) when they notoriously dispossessed the plaintiff erecting tin shed and wooden house on the suit land. As such, I find that the plaintiff was dispossessed by the defendants on 27.08.2000 and the suit has been filed within 12 years from such dispossession as required under Article 144 of the Limitation Act. As such, the suit cannot be considered as barred by limitation.
